Neonates of the Lazuli bunting emerge from eggs that have been incubated at a consistent temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], resulting in a hatching event that occurs approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] after the onset of incubation. At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings possess a remarkably modest wet weight of only 1.3 grams [Wwb = only 1.3 grams], a value reflecting the substantial yolk investment that has been metabolized during the embryonic period. This minimal body mass at emergence is characteristic of many small passerines and imposes a heavy energetic demand on the attending adults, who must provision the brood intensively to support rapid somatic growth. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, prior to any significant developmental water loss, averages 1.89 grams [Ww0 = averages 1.89 grams], indicating that the egg itself constitutes a relatively large proportion of the adult female's own mass. Field studies from the Sierra Nevada foothills have confirmed these values through repeated measurements of clutches in early spring, when ambient conditions still fluctuate considerably.

As the nestling period progresses, the developing chicks exhibit a steep growth trajectory driven by near-continuous parental provisioning. Within the thermal environment of a well-insulated nest, which often stabilizes around a core temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during brooding, the fledging event—defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest—occurs at approximately 12.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 12.5 days after hatching]. This relatively brief nestling phase is typical for altricial birds of this body size, placing a premium on efficient food delivery by both parents. The young birds leave the nest while still developing their flight feathers fully, and they remain dependent on their parents for several additional weeks. The pace of this early development is closely tied to the thermal conditions of the nest microenvironment; measurements taken from natural nests in California indicate that deviations from the typical brooding temperature can delay feather growth and motor coordination, underscoring the importance of consistent maternal attendance during the first week of life.

Following the rapid developmental phase of the nestling period, the juvenile birds enter a protracted stage of somatic growth and plumage maturation that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity. Under the thermal conditions typical of late spring and summer in their breeding range, with ambient temperatures frequently reaching 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during peak foraging hours, individuals generally reach puberty at an age of 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching]. This timing corresponds to the completion of the prebasic molt and the acquisition of definitive adult plumage, which in males is characterized by the vibrant azure blue coloration that gives the species its common name. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue from museum specimens show that spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females commence shortly after this age, confirming that the reproductive system becomes functionally competent. However, despite this early physiological readiness, most individuals do not initiate breeding activities during their first summer, deferring their first reproductive attempt to the following year.

The first breeding event for the Lazuli bunting is typically deferred until the spring following the year of hatching, a common life-history strategy among small migratory passerines that need to establish a territory and acquire sufficient body condition. Consequently, the age at first reproduction, measured as the time since birth at the laying of the first brood, is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This interval encompasses the autumn migration to wintering grounds in western Mexico, the overwintering period, and the northward return to breeding territories, all of which occur under varying thermal regimes. At the active metabolic temperatures typical of the breeding season, which average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during the hottest part of the day, the energetic costs of reproduction are substantial. Females produce clutches ranging from 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch], and in the most productive populations, they may attempt up to 1.5 clutches annually [F_R_i = up to 1.5 clutches annually], thereby maximizing their seasonal reproductive output in response to favorable resource pulses.

In terms of overall body size, adult Lazuli buntings demonstrate a modest degree of sexual dimorphism in mass, a pattern observed in many cardinalid finches. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, measured during the non-breeding season when they are not carrying eggs, averages 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams]. Males, which are slightly larger overall, achieve a somewhat greater asymptotic body mass of 15.4 grams [Wwi = 15.4 grams]. The lifespan of this species, as inferred from the oldest individuals recaptured during long-term banding studies in the Intermountain West, reaches up to 9.9 years [am = up to 9.9 years] under typical field cond at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]itions. At the active metabolic temperatures characteristic of their summer range, often around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during midday activity, the annual mortality rate appears to be balanced by the high reproductive output described above. Comparative analyses with other members of the genus Passerina suggest that these life-history parameters align with those of open-country congeners, with the slightly larger body mass of males likely conferring an advantage in territorial defense and mate acquisition.
